articles.title: RETRACTION: 3D Transparent Technology Displays the Developmental Patterns of Ductus Arteriosus Morphology in Chicken Embryos Before and After Birth.
articles.abstract: C. Xu, L. Li, X. Wu, Y. Zhang, C. Wu, J. Chen, H. Gao, and Z. Ma, "3D Transparent Technology Displays the Developmental Patterns of Ductus Arteriosus Morphology in Chicken Embryos Before and After Birth," Journal of Anatomy (Early View): https://doi.org/10.1111/joa.70126. The above article, published online on 06 March 2026 in Wiley Online Library (wileyonlinelibrary.com), has been retracted by agreement between the journal Editors-in-Chief, Phil Cox, James Sleigh, and Neil Vargesson; the Anatomical Society and John Wiley & Sons Ltd. Following publication, concerns were raised by a third party regarding Figures 1B and 1D-F. During a subsequent investigation, it was established that these images were published elsewhere in a different scientific context. Although the authors provided some original images, they were unable to provide a satisfactory explanation regarding the origin of the images or the discrepancies in the reported experimental conditions between this and the previous publication. The retraction has been agreed because the editors can no longer be confident in the reliability of the data and therefore consider the conclusions of this article to be invalid. The authors were informed of the retraction decision.

articles.title: Laryngeal branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve: A narrative review of human anatomical studies.
articles.authors: Daniel Goodman, Jordan Higgs, Robert T Sataloff
articles.abstract: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) provides motor innervation to all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid. Detailed knowledge of its terminal branching is essential for thyroid, laryngeal, and voice surgeons. This review synthesizes existing human cadaveric and surgical descriptions of the extralaryngeal and motor branching of the RLN, with attention to functional and clinical implications. Prior to laryngeal entry, the RLN most commonly bifurcates into an anterior (motor) and posterior (sensory) branch, with extralaryngeal branching identified in approximately 60% of nerves across large pooled series; bifurcation accounts for roughly half of all cases and typically occurs 1-2 cm inferior to the cricothyroid articulation. The motor division of the RLN is organized into vertical, genu, and oblique segments. The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle, the sole abductor of the true vocal fold, is innervated first and exhibits at least three distinct branching configurations, with further complexity arising from compartmental innervation patterns. The adductor muscles-arytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, and thyroarytenoid-are innervated sequentially, with the branches to the latter two representing the true terminal branches of the RLN. These branches form a complex anastomotic network with the superior laryngeal nerve, including Galen's anastomosis and the arytenoid plexus. Current anatomical knowledge derives predominantly from small cadaveric series; further studies are needed for characterization of these structures with greater resolution and clinical applicability.

articles.title: Topography of motor endplates in the human posterior cricoarytenoid muscle: Implications for selective reinnervation.
articles.authors: Aude Lagier, Valérie Defaweux, Joëlle Piret et al.
articles.abstract: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle (PCA) is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle that abducts the vocal fold and is therefore a key target for selective reinnervation in bilateral vocal fold paralysis. Because its distal nerve supply is anatomically variable, direct implantation strategies may benefit from precise knowledge of motor endplate topography. We characterized the spatial distribution of motor endplates in bilateral posterior cricoarytenoid muscles obtained from five human body donors (n = 5; four men and one woman; median age 80 years, range 79-98), yielding a total of 10 muscles for descriptive anatomical analysis. One left PCA was affected by documented unilateral vocal fold paralysis and was analyzed separately. Motor endplates were labeled with tetramethylrhodamine-conjugated α-bungarotoxin, imaged by whole-slide fluorescence scanning, and detected using a standardized QuPath workflow. In the nine muscles without known laryngeal pathology, motor endplates were heterogeneously distributed, with higher-density regions frequently forming an arcuate band. The vertical compartment contained a median of 71.5% of all detected endplates (range 52.8-87.3%) and showed a median areal density of 3.57 endplates/mm2, compared with 2.43 endplates/mm2 in the horizontal compartment. Muscle fibers bearing multiple motor endplates were also observed. The paralyzed PCA showed high motor endplate density across a broader portion of the muscle, with less clearly defined spatial zonation. These findings support the existence of preferential motor endplate zones in the human PCA, while highlighting substantial anatomical variability, particularly in the pathological specimen. This variability may have implications for the positioning of donor nerve implants during selective laryngeal reinnervation.

articles.title: Independent and joint associations of physical activity, sedentary behavior, and sleep with vitamin D status in US adults: a cross-sectional NHANES study.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Sha Li, Jie Feng, Junqiao Hu et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emerging evidence links movement behaviors to vitamin D status. This study investigated associations between physical activity (PA), sedentary behavior (SB), and sleep with vitamin D status and explored sex differences in these relationships. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 3195 adults (49.1 ± 17.1 years, 45.5% males) from the 2021-2023 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey with complete data. Self-reported PA, SB, and sleep duration were assessed. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D was measured using high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. Generalized linear and logistic regression models were performed. RESULTS: SB was negatively associated with vitamin D levels in the whole sample (β = -0.006; 95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.012, -0.001) and males (β = -0.008; 95% CI: -0.014, -0.002), but not females. Sleep duration was positively associated with vitamin D among males only (β = 0.023; 95% CI: 0.003, 0.043). Meeting both PA and SB guidelines showed the strongest and most consistent association with vitamin D sufficiency, observed across the whole sample (odds ratio [OR] = 2.129; 95% CI: 1.504, 3.012), males (OR = 2.013; 95% CI: 1.021, 3.967), and females (OR = 2.214; 95% CI: 1.360, 3.605). CONCLUSIONS: Movement behaviors demonstrate independent and joint associations with vitamin D status in US adults, with modest sex-specific patterns that warrant replication. Combined adherence to PA and SB guidelines was consistently associated with greater odds of vitamin D sufficiency across sexes.

articles.title: Novel creatine formulation exhibits similar serum creatine concentrations and pharmacokinetics to creatine monohydrate in healthy adults.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Gabrielle M DelBiondo, Celia W Gottlieb, Paul A Baker et al.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Creatine monohydrate (CrM) is the most widely studied creatine form, demonstrating robust efficacy, bioavailability, and safety. With creatine growing in popularity, alternative formulations of creatine have been developed to target solubility and to optimize absorption pharmacokinetics (PK), as well as to reduce gastrointestinal (GI) intolerability. The purpose of the current study was to evaluate the acute effects of a novel creatine monohydrate (OptiCreatineTM; CrO) compared to CrM on serum creatine PK and GI tolerability in healthy adults. METHODS: Healthy, recreationally active adults (age: 22 ± 3 years; males n = 8, females n = 9) consumed a single 5-gram dose of CrM or CrO across two separate visits following an overnight fast, in a randomized, double-blind, crossover design. Venous blood samples were collected at baseline and 30, 60, 90, 120, 180, 240, and 300 mins post-ingestion of their assigned treatment to assess serum creatine concentrations. PK parameters including peak concentration (Cmax), time to peak (Tmax), absorption rate constant (ka), elimination rate constant (kel; h-1), and area under the curve (AUC₀-T) were derived using nonlinear regression modeling. GI symptoms were assessed using validated questionnaires. RESULTS: There was no difference in serum creatine concentrations between CrM or CrO across all participants (p = 0.707), males (p = 0.318), or females (p = 0.996) at any time point. Serum creatine increased over time regardless of treatment (p < 0.0001). No differences were observed between CrM and CrO for Cmax (mean difference ± standard deviation (MD ± SD): 7.66 ± 50.37μM; p = 0.82), Tmax (MD ± SD: -0.04 ± 0.13 h; p = 0.54), ka (MD ± SD: -0.15 ± 0.45 h-1; p = 0.51), kel (MD ± SD: 0.01 ± 0.03 h-1; p = 0.61), or AUC₀-T (MD ± SD: 22.09 ± 160.57 μM·h; p = 0.74), with no sex × treatment interactions (p ≥ 0.05). Descriptive evaluation showed similar GI symptom profiles between conditions, with low frequency and minimal severity reported across both treatments. CONCLUSIONS: A single 5-gram dose of CrO produced similar serum creatine and PK characteristics to CrM in healthy adults. These findings support CrO as a viable delivery option, with no significant differences in acute pharmacokinetic profiles or GI tolerability compared to CrM.

articles.title: Dose-specific effects of caffeinated chewing gum on reactive blocking timing, jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses after volleyball-specific fatigue in elite female volleyball players.
articles.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
articles.authors: Jinghui Zhong, Jiyan Xu, Chang Lu et al.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the effects of caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 and 6 mg/kg on reactive blocking timing, block-jump mechanics, and neuromuscular responses in elite female volleyball players under post-fatigue conditions. METHODS: Fifteen elite female volleyball players completed a randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study implemented with double-blinding procedures. Participants consumed placebo (PLA), caffeinated chewing gum at nominal target doses of 3 mg/kg (CAF3) or 6 mg/kg (CAF6), and were tested after supplementation and warm-up at PRE and immediately after a volleyball-specific repeated blocking fatigue protocol (POST). Primary outcomes were reactive blocking timing-chain indices and block-jump (BJ) peak power. Secondary outcomes included additional BJ mechanical variables and general jump measures from countermovement jump (CMJ) and drop jump (DJ) tests. Exploratory outcomes included synchronized surface electromyography (sEMG) variables of lower-limb muscles. Participant blinding was assessed after each visit. RESULTS: Fatigue impaired jump-related performance across conditions (p < 0.05). For the primary outcomes, the descriptive decline in BJ peak power was 6.9% in CAF6 versus 13.9% in PLA; the adjusted POST comparison did not establish superiority of CAF6 over CAF3. For timing outcomes, overall sequence time increased by 18.4% in PLA, 6.4% in CAF3, and 3.0% in CAF6; CAF6 therefore showed the smallest descriptive deterioration in the integrated sequence measure, whereas CAF3 showed little change in the mean stationary and movement component times. CAF6 showed a reduction in mean stationary response time and the smallest increase in overall sequence time. For secondary outcomes, caffeine showed more favorable post-fatigue responses in selected CMJ/DJ measures, including CMJ mean propulsive power and DJ contact time (p < 0.05), and CAF6 showed greater preservation of selected stretch-shortening cycle-related mechanical measures, including DJ jump height and DJ vertical stiffness, than PLA (p < 0.05). In contrast, CMJ mRSI showed a divergent pattern and was not interpreted as evidence of caffeine-related attenuation of fatigue-induced decrements. Exploratory sEMG results showed smaller post-fatigue changes in selected frequency-domain and activation-timing variables under CAF6, particularly in measures related to extensor-muscle function. Participant masking was incomplete: perceived caffeine ingestion was reported in 0.0%, 53.3%, and 80.0% of PLA, CAF3, and CAF6 visits, respectively, and adverse effects were more frequent in CAF6. CONCLUSIONS: The observed responses were outcome-specific: CAF6 showed a smaller decline in BJ peak power and the smallest increase in overall sequence time, whereas CAF3 showed little change in mean stationary and movement response times. These findings do not establish a generally preferable dose or a timing-stability advantage for CAF3. Incomplete participant masking limits attribution of the differences exclusively to caffeine dose.

articles.title: Dietary potassium intake from different food sources and mortality in maintenance haemodialysis patients: a multicentre prospective cohort study.
articles.authors: Chaoying Xia, Ziyang You, Zhen Wen et al.
articles.abstract: The association between dietary potassium intake and mortality in maintenance haemodialysis (MHD) patients remains controversial, particularly regarding potassium from different dietary sources. In this multicentre prospective cohort study, dietary potassium intake was assessed using 24-hour dietary recalls. Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Restricted cubic splines assessed dose-response relationships, and sensitivity analyses included adjustment for dietary quality indicators, exclusion of serum potassium, exclusion of deaths within the first year, and competing-risk models. The lowest tertile of total dietary potassium intake was associated with higher all-cause mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR]: 1·36, 95 % CI: 1·02-1·81). The lowest tertile of plant-based potassium intake was associated with increased all-cause mortality (aHR: 1·54, 95% CI: 1·19-1·99) and cardiovascular mortality (aHR: 1·50, 95% CI: 1·05-2·14). Restricted cubic spline analyses demonstrated inverse dose-response relationships between total dietary potassium intake and both mortality outcomes and between plant-based potassium intake and all-cause mortality. Dietary potassium intake was not associated with serum potassium levels or hyperkalaemia risk, whereas severe hyperkalaemia (serum potassium ≥6·0 mmol/L) independently predicted cardiovascular mortality (aHR: 1·59, 95% CI: 1·06-2·38). Lower dietary potassium intake, particularly from plant sources, was associated with increased mortality risk among MHD patients. These findings support a more individualised approach to dietary potassium management in MHD patients.
